On Jan 4, 2007, at 4:14 PM, Dan Tenenbaum wrote:

Yes.


> I am using Rserve via the Java client, JRclient.
>
> I want to call an R method that takes a matrix as a parameter, and  
> I want to use the parameter binding facilities of Rconnection  
> rather than passing the matrix as a literal. How do I do that?
>

I'm assuming that you want to create a matrix in R from data values  
in Java without using the string representation [Rconnection doesn't  
really have parameter binding]. This can be done in several ways, but  
probably the most efficient one is to create an array containing all  
the values, assign it to R and create a matrix from it, i.e.  
something like:

double d[] = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 , 6 };

re.assign("a", d);
re.voidEval("a<-matrix(a, 3)")

The resulting variable "a" will look like this:

      [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    4
[2,]    2    5
[3,]    3    6

Cheers,
Simon

> 3. invoke the R program with extracted parameters
> 4. from within the Java program collect the return values and

Yes


> Is it possible for objects to be shared between JRI and rJava.
> For example, can I have the R program update the Java object  
> (theObj) with the results using RJava?

Yes - they are sharing the same JVM. JRI and rJava are essentially  
one interface - each for one direction - so you can mix them as you  
wish.


> How do I get the reference to the shared Java object?
>

I'm not quite sure what you mean - you are dealing with one JVM, so a  
Java object is accessible both from R and Java automatically and  
simultaneously, there is no conversion necessary. Also note that Java  
objects are always references, so R never creates a copy of an object  
(the R representation may get copied, but it is always a reference to  
the same Java object - see the concept of external references in R).

Cheers,
Simon

messages.body_plain:
Simon,

On Jan 10, 2007, at 11:18 AM, Simon Pears wrote:

> If I source an R program from a file how do I access the Java  
> object from within the R program using RJava.
> .jnew is redundant since it creates a reference to a newly  
> constructred R object within the R program.

That is not quite true - it creates a new Java object (not R object!)  
in the JVM, so you're free to use such object as your shared object  
if you wish.


> .jcall could be used from witihin the R program. From the HTML help  
> file it's signature is given as:
>
> .jcall(obj, returnSig = "V", method, ..., evalArray = TRUE,
>    evalString = TRUE, check = TRUE, interface = "RcallMethod")
>
> However, how do I retrieve the reference/pointer to obj from within  
> the R program using R Java? Do I have to use an R base library to  
> retrieve this?
>
> Is there any example code for retrieving references to Java objects  
> that exist in the client JRI program that invoked R?
>

It really depends on your exact implementation. As stated above, you  
can create such an object via .jnew, but there are other ways.  
Probably the simplest way is to use a static  field:
public class Foo {
public static Object sharedObject;
}

o <- .jfield("Foo", "sharedObject")

An alternative way is to use low-level RNI, namely rniJavaToXref:
re.rniAssign("o", re.rniJavaToXref(o), 0);
re.eval("o <- new('jobjRef', jobj=o)", false);

However, rniJavaToXref is not public, so you'll have to make it  
public in JRI first and for the simple application here I'd recommend  
to not fiddle with RNI as it is really low-level.

Cheers,
Simon

Simon,

On Jan 11, 2007, at 6:08 AM, Simon Pears wrote:

> I am a "newbie" to R and JRI.
> I have written a very small simple test script that I want to  
> source and invoke from JRI. The R script is as follows:
>
> #test.R script
> a<-2
> b<-1
> c<-a+b
>
> print(c)
>
>
> I am invoking this from JRI as :
>
> // j_eng is REngine
> REXP exp = j_eng.eval ("source('c:/TEMP/test.R')");
> System.out.println(exp);
>
>
> The output from this is:
> Result = RXP[unknown/19, id=187344944, o=null]
>
>
> When I do this from an R terminal I get the output [1] 3.
> How do I retrieve this result using JRI?
>

First, you should understand the concepts involved here. When you are  
using the R console (like in the terminal), it runs a REPL: read -  
evaluate - print loop. The Rengine's eval method gives you the  
"evaluate" part, so it doesn't use console input (read) or output  
(print) per se. If you want to provide an interactive console, you'll  
have to implement callbacks that handle calls from R concerning read/ 
print - see the rtest.java example for a simple implementation of the  
callback interface.

However, in your case I suspect this is not what you really want. If  
all you need is to run a computation in R and get the result, then  
you want to get the raw result and not some string representation.  
Therefore your example above may look more like:

REXP exp = j_eng.eval("{a<-2; b<-1; a+b}");
System.out.println(exp.asDouble());

Clearly, you can evaluate any R expressions, so you can as well use  
capture.output to suppress any console output and return it as a  
string value, so you can run something like this:

REXP exp = j_eng.eval("paste(capture.output({a<-2; b<-1; print(a 
+b)}),collapse='\\n')");
System.out.println(exp.asString());

This allows you to capture R on per-expression basis if desired.  
Again, this may or may not be what you want for a given problem.  
String representation is very inefficient for further processing. At  
any rate it should give you an idea on what your options are.

Cheers,
Simon

Dan,

this actually the standard behavior in a unix shell, so you shouldn't  
be surprised ;). When you start a process from the shell in the  
background, the shell will still send HUP to it when it closes and it  
will wait for its children to close. This is why the shell appears to  
hang and yet Rserve gets closed. It is advisable to use `nohup' if  
you want to run it from a shell and be able to close the shell  
without shutting down Rserve.
In a sense I understand your confusion, because some other daemons  
use HUP for other purposes (e.g. reloading configuration), but Rserve  
doesn't.

Cheers,
Simon

messages.body_plain:
Ido,

On Jan 26, 2007, at 5:57 AM, Ido M. Tamir wrote:

> ist it possible to reinitialize a jvm from R?
>

Currently, no. There is an undocumented internal C function that  
attempts to destroy the JVM:
.C("doneJVM")
You can try it (you get a list of error as explained below), but  
you're entirely on your own - your platform may not even allow you to  
create another VM at all.

One of the main reasons for not providing .jexit is that R holds  
references to several internal objects in Java, so destroying the VM  
makes all those references invalid (including all objects that you  
created until garbage collected). The second reason is that you need  
to detach all threads first, but R has no idea what threads you  
created (you could have done it in Java code or indirectly, e.g. by  
calling AWT/Swing).


> After I made some changes to my java function, I always have to  
> make a new R session to pick up the changes.
> Is there something like .jexit?
> detaching rJava did not help.
>
> Also: where is this jvm instance actually, because I can not find  
> it with ps ax etc...  Even if I kill all java processes the .jcall  
> still works.
>

java processes have nothing to do with it - there is just one  
process: the R process.

Cheers,
Simon

messages.body_plain:
Craig,


On Jan 30, 2007, at 2:16 PM, Craig Macdonald wrote:

> I've recently installed R, and liked the look of your JGR GUI, so  
> decided to give that
> a whirl too.
> On my Fedora Core 3 desktop (non root), I built and installed R  
> using --enable-R-shlib option, and can confirm that libR.so is  
> built. Our local java install is Sun jdk1.5.0_09
>
> However, I have problems using JGR. Essentially, R is started, but  
> it is unable to dyn.load() any other libraries, (including  
> grDevices.so and methods.so), due to undefined symbols.
>

are you sure that you're picking up the right R and packages? You  
must re-compile all packages for your newly built R. The errors look  
as if you have mismatch between various parts of R. Please make sure  
that you are dealing only with one R version here. Also verify that  
JRI is picking up the correct R version at compile time. Please send  
me the config and compile logs if in doubt.

But first, let's go one step back - are you sure you need your own  
version of R? I have reports from many people using FC that use R  
with shared library from rpms, without the need to re-compile. Once  
you have multiple R versions in your system, you must be very careful  
that everything is configured correctly.

Cheers,
Simon
